text:
TCP is connection-oriented and reliable; UDP is connectionless and best-effort.

**TCP** sets up a connection (three-way handshake) and guarantees that data arrives, in order, without duplicates. It does this with sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission, and flow and congestion control. The cost is extra latency, per-connection state, and head-of-line blocking: one lost packet stalls everything behind it until it is retransmitted. It delivers a byte stream with no message boundaries.

**UDP** just sends individual datagrams. There is no handshake, no delivery or ordering guarantee, no retransmission, and no congestion control. Packets may be lost, duplicated, or reordered, and the application must deal with that if it cares. The header is 8 bytes versus TCP's 20+, and it preserves message boundaries.

Use TCP when correctness matters (HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, SSH, email, file transfer, databases). Use UDP when latency matters more than completeness or when you want your own transport logic (DNS, VoIP, games, live video, and QUIC/HTTP/3, which builds reliability and congestion control on top of UDP).
